Five heatwaves between May and August left the majority of the country in drought and have sparked wildfires and travel disruption.

Solar panels can cut the amount of electricity you need to buy from the grid and give you more control over how your home uses energy. But getting the most from them involves more than simply choosing a set of panels and putting them on the roof.
Everything from the amount of shade your roof receives to when you use electricity – and what happens to the power you don’t use – can affect how well a solar installation works for your household. Batteries and smart energy tariffs can make a difference too.
If you’re thinking about going solar, keep reading to discover the seven things worth knowing before the installers arrive.

1. Shade matters more than you expect
A bit of light research into solar installation will inform you about the importance of roof orientation and pitch, but one area that doesn’t always come up is shade – and even partial shading can affect how much electricity you generate at certain times of day.
Trees, chimneys, neighbouring buildings and even roof features can reduce output during specific hours. A good installer will assess shading properly before you commit, so it’s worth making sure this forms part of your initial survey rather than assuming ideal conditions. Octopus Energy will assess levels of shading, then recommend the right tech for the job. For shadier roofs, for example, optimised microinverters can be fitted, which move the power conversion from a single central point to the individual panel level, allowing each panel to work independently of the others, maximising energy production.

2. A home battery can help you use more of your solar energy
One of the biggest surprises for new solar owners is how much electricity they generate when they’re not at home. If everyone’s out during the day, much of that power is exported back to the grid. A home battery helps make the most of this surplus by storing energy so it can be used later: in the evening, overnight, or during peak periods. With a smart import and export tariff, a battery can also be charged from the grid when electricity is cheaper, while surplus stored energy can potentially be exported when rates are higher.
Even if a battery isn’t installed straight away, thinking about it early can help future-proof your setup. Choosing compatible equipment, inverters and tariffs can make upgrades far simpler, particularly as electric vehicles, heat pumps and flexible energy pricing become more common.

The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action.

As the death toll continues to mount – the latest count showed more than 900 dead and more than 4,400 individuals missing – this event has crystalized the climate crisis for many.
One reason is undoubtedly the sheer horror of what unfolded here. Chilling surveillance and eyewitness footage captured the horrific moment a 40mph wall of “liquid concrete” violently overtook fleeing crowds, instantly swallowing entire families and burying them beneath feet of thick, red-soaked silt. Another reason, however, is that the connection with climate change was unassailable in this case.






The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all
Nesrine Malik

The torrent was the direct result of warming-induced glacial collapse, which dumped millions of tons of rock, unleashing a high-velocity wave of mud and debris. The new reality in the era of human-caused climate change, a CNN headline put it, is that “living downstream from a glacier has become a deadly liability”.
The impact of climate change on extreme weather, by contrast, is usually established though a statistical, rather than direct causal, connection. Through what is known as attribution science, climate scientists demonstrate the influence of climate change on the characteristics of an extreme weather event. It is analogous to how epidemiologists establish a linkage between cause (eg smoking cigarettes) and effect (lung cancer), through massive statistical evidence.

Flash flooding in Arizona tourist destination was likely triggered by compounding climate factors, such as drought and warming in Pacific Ocean 
 
 
Remote Grand Canyon lodge hit by deadly flash flood boasts fabled history 











A deadly flash flood in the Grand Canyon over the weekend was likely driven by a confluence of climate factors, including drought, wildfire scarring and warming temperatures in the Pacific Ocean that can supercharge storms.
At least two people have died, nearly 80 people were rescued and one remained unaccounted for after a surge of water and debris swept through the immensely popular tourist destination on Saturday, fueled by torrents of rain that hit the national park’s Bright Angel Creek area.




 
 
Flash floods are not uncommon in the region, especially during the monsoon season from June to September, when strong rains pummel the arid landscapes and can quickly fill narrow rock formations. Visiting the Grand Canyon – a crown jewel of the US national park system – can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding, when clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
The steep, rocky nature of the canyon itself funnels water rapidly, transforming downpours into a charging wall of water.


View image in fullscreen
This handout image released by the National Park Service shows a storm system moving across the North Rim of Grand Canyon national park on 29 August. Photograph: J Baird/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images
But Saturday’s strong storm also hit part of the burn scar of the Dragon Bravo wildfire, a destructive and fast-moving blaze that swept across nearly 150,000 acres (60,700 hectares) and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge in July 2025.
Runoff tends to flow more quickly in the aftermath of a fire, especially in hotter burns where slopes are left barren of vegetation.
While it’s still unclear how directly long-term damage to the landscape from that fire played a role in last weekend’s disaster, federal models indicated a rise in the risks of debris flows in Bright Angel Creek.





Floods sweeping through Grand Canyon national park
Teams with the Department of Interior charged to assess post-fire threats to “life, property, and critical natural and cultural resources”, found runoff risks would be between two and eight times greater upstream of Phantom Creek. “Hikers on the trails within or downslope from the burned area will experience frequent stabilization issues, especially hazardous rockfall for at least the first year,” the team wrote in a report on conditions.
Park officials were reportedly concerned at the start of this summer that stronger storms could create dangerous conditions near the burned areas. Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’




The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution.
UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics.

With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues.
Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.”


Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused on plastic microfibres from synthetic textiles.
Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.
Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.”
She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring. Heat pumps are fast becoming one of the most talked-about, low-carbon alternatives to gas boilers in UK homes. Very simply, they work by extracting heat from the air or ground outside and using it to warm your home and hot water. Unlike a boiler, where the temperature can yo-yo, a heat pump will keep your home at a constant temperature and running costs can be lower. 
As interest grows, companies such as Octopus Energy have played a role in bringing heat pumps into the mainstream, offering installation services for homeowners looking to switch. But despite their rising popularity, heat pumps are still widely misunderstood. From concerns about cold weather performance to expensive installation, a number of myths continue to circulate. “Heat pumps don’t work in cold weather”
Not true. Heat pumps are designed to extract heat from the air even when temperatures drop as low as -20C. 





Admittedly, on the rare days it does get cold in the UK, a heat pump will need to work harder and use more electricity to capture and compress that heat. However, it still delivers more heat energy than the electricity it consumes. A heat pump typically produces around three to four units of heat for every one unit of electricity used. 
By comparison, a gas boiler generates heat by burning fuel, with some energy lost through combustion and flue gases and typically operates at around 85 to 95 per cent efficiency. 

“Heat pumps have to be on south-facing walls”
A myth. Heat pumps can in fact be installed on any external wall, provided there is enough space and airflow around the unit. Other factors such as pipe runs, noise considerations and access for maintenance are far more important than the direction the unit faces.

“Heat pumps can replace air conditioning in heatwaves”
Yes, and no; it depends on the type of heat pump you have. Most heat pumps installed in UK homes are air-to-water systems; some models can offer cooling as well as heating, but it is not a standard feature.


If you're looking for both heating and air conditioning, an air-to-air heat pump is the better option, although they are less commonly fitted in the UK. If cooling is a priority, it's worth discussing the best heat pump for your home with your installer.

Andy Burnham should call a cross-party meeting to discuss the UK’s response to worsening extreme weather, including the forthcoming ‘super El Niño’, the Liberal Democrats have said.
The prime minister chaired a Cobra emergency meeting on the drought earlier this month but there has been little from the government on the wider threats posed by five successive heatwaves since May and expected global issues with food shortages and inflation.

Heylings and Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, wrote to Burnham a fortnight ago, proposing a meeting of the UK’s party leaders “to discuss the long-term measures needed to protect our country from climate impacts and build resilience to the extreme weather we are already experiencing”. Heylings contrasted Burnham’s reluctance to address the climate crisis with his prioritising of social care, on which he has called for cross-party support: “We want the same approach [to the climate].”

It’s hard to believe that a mountain range as mighty as the Himalayas can actually be fragile and increasingly unstable, but the avalanches, landslides and floods that have always shaped and scoured the valleys are now in overdrive as temperatures rise twice as fast in Nepal as the global average.



Hotter conditions mean that the ice that acts as a glue to bind the rocks is now melting. Giant glaciers are being diminished and weakened, and frozen soil, known as permafrost, is thawing.





The result is that a region home to important shrines for Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims and popular destinations for climbers and trekkers is becoming more volatile. 



Inevitably, this raises questions about whether it’s possible for the Nepalese to live safely in a landscape that’s sacred but unpredictable – and how to advise visitors about when, or even whether, they should go.

A massive chunk of ice and rock crashed into the valley below with enough force to set off earthquake alarms. That created a tsunami of water, mud and debris, which surged down a string of valleys known as the Bhoti Koshi-Trishuli corridor, tearing bridges and buildings from their foundations.

Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global supplies


Organisers say people must revive spiritual relationship with food amid double threat of climate crisis and conflict




Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven weather extremes will require more than economic fixes and intensive agriculture, according to the organisers of a pioneering summit this week, who say the world must revive its spiritual relationship with food.
Delegates from more than 60 countries and the UN will gather for the next five days in Paro in the tiny Himalayan nation of Bhutan for the world’s first “conscious food summit”, which will bring together governments and farmers, mindfulness experts and yoga therapists.

Tshering Tobgay, Bhutan’s prime minister, said: “Food lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time – hunger, poor nutrition, poverty, climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasingly food security is also being disrupted by conflict and geopolitical instability. Our central message is simple: transforming our food systems requires both inner and outer change.”
Conscious eating is at the heart of these talks, which will promote regenerative practices and Indigenous knowledge. “Consciousness can cultivate compassion, empathy, resilience, creativity and a stronger connection with nature,” Tobgay said in an interview with the Guardian. “This does not mean choosing spirituality over science. It means recognising that our values and mindsets influence how science, policy, finance and technology are used.”

‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks


Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas




Turkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough.
Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide and causes 25% of global heating today. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”.

The Guardian revealed in 2023 that Turkmenistan was the worst country for methane mega-leaks. Sources in Turkmenistan said this scrutiny was the “critical step” in leading the secretive and authoritarian government to engage with foreign partners.
A “super-emitter” leak, the escape of tonnes of methane per hour from a single valve or pipeline, heats the planet more than the emissions from a million SUVs or an entire coal-fired power station.
Turkmenistan had now stopped eight leaks by repairing corroded pipes, faulty wells and failing flares. The work was an “incredible first step”, said the UN, but much remained to be done.


View image in fullscreen
A satellite image of a methane leak in Turkmenistan’s Lebap province, which was plugged in March after a corroded pipe was fixed. Illustration: UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory


The UN Methane Alert and Response System (Mars) sent 192 alerts of methane plumes to Turkmenistan in the last year. The country had three of the six worst leaks detected in the world by Mars in last six months, and nine of the top 50.
Turkmenistan responded to about 20% of the alerts with on-the-ground information about the leaks and potential plans to fix them. In contrast, the US was sent the second highest number of alerts – 138 – but responded to none and had fixed no leaks in the last year. Other nations that failed to respond to any alerts were Iran, Russia and China.

The worst methane leak detected was an extraordinary leak in Mexico’s offshore oil and gas industry of 37 tonnes per hour, equivalent to the emissions of more than 7m SUVs. Mexico responded to all 23 Mars alerts in the last year, but had yet to complete a fix.

articles.jina_text:
Richer countries might have more resources to deal with catastrophe, but this problem grips the entire planet, however much leaders may want to deny it





Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.

Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. Wesley Morgan for the Conversation





Climate change is the greatest threat to the Pacific, with fuel shortages and missile tests also on the agenda as Anthony Albanese heads to Palau





Anthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annual Pacific Islands Forum and regional security is expected to top the agenda.

And as the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.
But the forum will be missing key leaders – Solomon Islands’ prime minister, Matthew Wale, made a shock departure, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home.

The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains

Editorial





Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution





The alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, China blocked exports of key rare earths to Japan in a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about 70% of rare-earth mining globally and 90% of separation and processing.
Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, has already jumped because of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.



The 17 metals known as rare earths are far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing are costly, complex and often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedly flowing to Asia because of the lack of domestic demand. While “Big shovel” is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worth less than $6bn globally last year.

articles.jina_text:
People have been warned to stay away from a popular beauty spot pond used for swimming and other water sports due to "hidden hazards" exposed by reduced water levels.
Keepers Pond in Abergavenny poses "serious safety risks" with levels dangerously low, according to Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, also known as the Brecon Beacons.
It said that along with the prolonged dry spell, the water had been used to tackle recent wildfires.
"As the water has receded, previously hidden hazards and unknown objects have been exposed on the pond bed, creating serious safety risks. For your own safety, you must not enter the water under any circumstances," the park authority said in a Facebook post.

Getty Images
Keepers Pond (pictured in 2020) is ordinarily a popular spot for swimming and water sports
The restriction applies to all activities on or in the water, including swimming, paddleboarding, kayaking, and any other water-based activities.
"We ask that visitors respect the area and do not remove, disturb or interfere with any objects or features revealed by the low water levels," it said.
The beauty spot car park remains open to visitors but "for your own safety", the national park said, "you must not enter the water under any circumstances".

The Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning stretching from south-west England and parts of Wales across the Midlands to eastern England. The warning will be in force from midday until 9pm on Saturday.



The forecaster warned of a risk of flash flooding after an unusually dry summer, with travellers told to expect longer journey times as the rain sets in for the weekend, with England, Wales and Northern Ireland observing a bank holiday on Monday.

“Some places could see an inch of rain in less than an hour,” Dewhurst said. “This is likely to lead to surface flooding, it could lead to some surface water on the roads.”



He also warned that while places within the yellow warning zone will experience the “most intense” rainfall, other areas are going to be very wet this weekend, with heavy rain expected from the west of England to Wales and Northern Ireland on Saturday.

A team of specially trained crisis response staff from the UK are arriving in Nepal, alongside £5million in humanitarian support sent by the British government. 
Some 3,700 people have been rescued so far on the Nepalese side following the glacier collapse. 
However rescuers remain on high alert, amid warnings that a new lake formed at high altitude in the Himalayas may be on the verge of overflowing. 
The lake has reduced in depth by 10 metres from when it peaked on Thursday, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported. 
Helicopters are continuing to bring in essential aid, including clothes and food essentials such as rice, crackers and instant noodles. 
 
   
Armed police search a disaster site with sniffer dogs in Devighat, Nuwakot district in Nepal (Picture: Reuters) 
Among the evacuated were several young babies, carried to safety in the arms of soldiers. 
Most of those rescued were only carrying the clothes they were wearing and, in some cases, a small plastic bag. 
In Nuwakot, one of the communities deeply affected by the flooding, a list of dozens of missing people was pinned to the wall of a relief centre. 
Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said his relatives had been ‘swept away’ by the floods. 
He said the country was paying the price for global warming and that the disaster had wreaked an ‘irreplaceable loss’ on communities.

More than a dozen states have considered moratoria on datacentres. New York became the first US state to enact a temporary ban last month. Progressive stalwarts Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a national moratorium. And even Greg Abbott, the far-right governor of Texas, called for a ban on datacentre development in rural swaths of his state.

Fuelling alarm about datacentres are environmental concerns over water usage and toxic contamination, as well as worries about the kind of society that the artificial-intelligence technologies powered by the new datacentres are creating.



Another of the most politically potent objections strikes closer to the wallet: data centres require enormous amounts of electricity, and that increase in demand can drive up utility bills.
More on datacentres’ impact on electricity costs after this week’s most important reads …
Essential reads
 
 
‘Our new normal’: how marine heatwaves affect life in British seas 
 
Iraq’s ghost villages: Islamic State drove people away – now a new enemy is preventing their return 
 
Destroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the Danube 
In focus


View image in fullscreen
Demonstrators participate in a nationwide protest against data centres in Virginia, July 2026.  Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Larbert residents group


A stunning seven out of 10 Americans are opposed to the construction of datacentres for artificial intelligence in their area, a major poll found in May, with 48% saying they are strongly opposed. About one-fifth of participants specifically pointed to possible negative financial consequences associated with datacentres as a reason for their opposition, including the potential for higher utility bills.
The backlash has created a bind for the Trump administration, which wants the US to become the world leader in artificial intelligence, but has also promised to bring down electricity bills. The US president’s answer so far has been the “Ratepayer Protection Pledge”, a voluntary agreement that he claims will keep families from footing the bill for the AI boom. Nearly 200 companies, utilities, datacentre developers and states signed on to the agreement, the administration announced last month.
The pledge asks datacentre developers and artificial intelligence firms to agree to cover the costs of the electricity they use and the new infrastructure needed to connect their facilities to the grid. The problem, critics say, is that the pledge has no teeth. It is not legally binding, and there are no clear consequences for companies that fail to follow through.
Green groups have been particularly unimpressed: Patrick Drupp, climate policy director at the Sierra Club, last month called it a “paper-thin commitment” for families struggling with their bills, and Lena Moffitt, executive director of nonprofit Evergreen Action, described the announcement as a mere “photo op with big tech”.

Decision to rescind ‘roadless rule’ opens more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging




More than 400 endangered animal and plant species could face accelerated extinction after the Donald Trump administration’s decision to rescind a rule that has protected old-growth forests for more than two decades.
According to a new report from the Center for Biological Diversity, the rollback of the Bill Clinton-era “roadless rule” could put 7.4m acres (3m hectares) of endangered-species habitat and nearly 1,800 miles (2,900km) of protected rivers and streams at risk, while opening more than 45m acres of national forests to roads, drilling and logging.

The Trump administration moved last week to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, citing “outdated restrictions [that] have kept tens of millions of forested acres off-limits to the very treatments that improve forest health and reduce wildfire risk to our communities”.


View image in fullscreen
An American black bear at Glacier national park in Montana. Photograph: Frank Fichtmüller/Getty Images
Conservationists have criticized the decision.


“Our national forests are home to some of America’s most iconic animals, from grizzlies to hellbenders. These forests provide clean drinking water to countless communities. Bulldozing more roads through them will mean dirtier water, fragmented wildlife habitat and greater wildfire risk,” said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity.







Trump administration to rescind rule protecting old-growth forests

At-risk species include grizzly bears and gray wolves in the Rocky Mountains, wild salmon in the Pacific north-west and Alaska, Mexican spotted owls and Gila trout in the south-west, as well as rare butterflies and wildflowers nationwide, according to the report.
In the Rocky Mountains, 9.7m acres of roadless areas are at risk, including 2.9m acres of critical habitat and nearly 11,000 miles of streams home to 21 imperiled plant and animal species. Montana’s roadless areas also protect watersheds supplying drinking water to communities in Bozeman, the Flathead valley and the Seeley-Swan valley, the report found.
In Alaska, the rollback threatens wild salmon in the 9.3m-acre Tongass national forest, which produces more wild salmon than any other national forest. The region’s $1bn-a-year commercial and sport fishing economy which accounts for one in 10 jobs in south-east Alaska may also be affected, the report noted.

Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis

Sunil Acharya






Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states


Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, Nepal





As a Nepali citizen working on international climate policy for more than a decade, it is difficult to look at the harrowing images coming out of the catastrophic flash flood that thundered down valleys in Nepal, sweeping down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, and not feel angry.
Not just because of the destruction, but because it comes after years of warnings from scientists and civil society that a rapidly warming planet would make disasters more frequent, more intense and harder to predict. This is what the cost of delaying global climate action looks like.

On 26 August, a wall of ice, water, rock and mud tore through communities, destroying homes, markets, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of people were killed and many more remain missing. The devastation came with terrifying speed. For people living along the rivers and the tourists trekking in the hills, there was little time between the hazard emerging high in the mountains and destruction reaching the valleys below.
The immediate questions are rightly being asked about what happened and whether people could have been warned. Nepal needs stronger early warning systems, better monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, cross-border communication between Nepal and Tibet and greater investment in preparedness.
But Nepal’s flash floods expose something more fundamental: the problem is not the absence of a warning system – it is a climate crisis that is producing hazards that behave differently from those the systems were designed to detect.

The sudden, debris-laden flood destroyed upstream hydrological stations before they could register a rising water level and trigger an alert. The system was designed to detect a more gradual rise in water levels. This flood arrived as a massive surge of rock, mud and water, destroying the very instruments meant to detect it.

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates 
 
What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet? 




The devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal and Tibet has heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.
Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.

A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2.
“Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,” the US Geological Survey said.

The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution.
Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but many observe that glaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal.


View image in fullscreen
Flooding in the Bhotekoshi River has affected low-lying areas along the riverbanks and nearby homes in Nuwakot, Nepal.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
The detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together.
Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site.
“These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre.

A series of strong El Niño climatic patterns in recent decades, such as the “Godzilla” event currently brewing that is set to warp weather around the world, have been supercharged by the broader overheating of the planet caused by the burning of fossil fuels, a major new study has found.
El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon, taking place every two to seven years, when the waters of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean heat up, causing a cascade of impacts around the world. The latest developing El Niño, set to peak later this year, is set to be the strongest in living memory and has been informally dubbed a “Godzilla” event.

It’s well understood that El Niño, which typically brings a surge of global heat, further amplifies the escalating climate crisis, with next year almost certain to be the hottest on record globally. But the new research has established that the reverse is also the case: human-caused global heating is making El Niño itself more intense when it does arrive.


“Our findings suggest El Niño can supercharge global warming but also global warming can supercharge El Niño – that is what we are seeing,” said Julia Cole, a climate researcher at the University of Michigan, who led the new study, published in Science.







‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn

Read more
“We are seeing a trend of stronger El Niños and the one we have now is consistent with that trend – it’s not a fluke. We are seeing a shift where El Niño doesn’t look like what it did prior to industrial times. That is bad news for climate hazards and for people, particularly those who are badly impacted and yet have done little to cause climate change.”
As the world has heated up due to the use of fossil fuels, a string of recent “super” El Niño events has provided extra acceleration, with intense events causing the global temperature record to fall in 1998, then 2016 and then further in 2024.
Such strong El Niño episodes have become far more common as overall global temperatures have risen, scientists found in the new research, which painstakingly analyzed the composition of large boulder-like deposits of coral fossils found on the Galápagos Islands.
These old corals, which date to 1,000 years ago, contain chemical compositions that indicate what the sea surface temperature was like when they were alive. The Galápagos, situated off the coast of mainland Ecuador, is “right in the heart of El Niño country”, Cole said, where surrounding waters heat up during such an event.
While El Niños remained fairly stable for most of this long period, things started to change around the time the world started to mass industrialize in the late 19th century. This process has become even more extreme in the past 40 years, with El Niños’ variability now around 37% higher than during preindustrial times.

Your questions answered on solar panels
Plug-in solar panels can legally go on sale in the UK from today, 27 August, giving households a new way to generate electricity without paying thousands of pounds for a conventional rooftop solar installation.
The rule change allows compliant systems with an AC output of up to 800W to be connected directly to a suitable household socket. Unlike a traditional solar array, these smaller systems can be installed by the homeowner and positioned in a garden or, where the rules allow, on a wall or balcony. However, only products that meet the government’s new plug-in solar device interim product specification qualify under the new rules. 
And, for the first time, there are now compliant products that you can actually order. UKSOL has secured compliant listings on the Energy Networks Association’s Connect Direct register for its plug-in solar pro range. Retailers such as City Plumbing have begun listing its first ground-mounted systems. 
Other big-name retailers, including B&Q, Currys, Amazon and Lidl, have been working with the government on the introduction of plug-in solar, although they have yet to announce complete ranges of their own. 
We’ll be covering the plug-in solar launch live throughout the day, bringing you the latest product announcements, prices, retailer availability, safety advice and reaction as it happens.

Where can you buy plug-in solar panels now? 
The first compliant plug-in solar systems are beginning to appear online. Argos is the first UK retailer to sell plug-in panels online, with prices from £599. It has listed five models that meet the full requirements for the new plug-in solar compliance, all from UKSOL. These kits come complete with everything you need to get started; you just need to set them up and plug them into a standard AC socket.
The cheapest kit currently available to buy at Argos is £599 and is the UKSOL 515W pro compact plug-in solar with hybrid mount bundle. It offers a 515W single solar panel system with adjustable mounting options. The panel then plugs into the 800W microinverter, which can connect via wifi or Bluetooth to the monitoring app on a mobile device. The small microinverter is IP67-rated, so you can leave it outside and run the supplied 4m cable into the house or apartment to plug in.
Aside from Argos, City Plumbing currently lists UKSOL kits, and the brand is also selling systems direct. Other specialist retailers are beginning to list UKSOL systems too.

Symptoms of giardiasis 
According to the NHS, symptoms of the condition include: 
 
smelly diarrhoea 
stomach pain or cramps 
flatulence 
smelly burps – which may smell like eggs 
bloating 
weight loss  
‘The infection itself can last around a week, however there are some cases where symptoms have persisted for several weeks and even months,’ Daniel Turnbull, professional standards pharmacist at Pharmacy2U tells Metro. 
‘This is an important reminder to why ongoing diarrhoea should not be ignored.; 
How it spreads 
As Hanna Yusuf, prescribing pharmacist at Chemist4U, explains, giardiasis is transmitted ‘primarily through contact with infected people or animals, as well as ingesting contaminated food, water and drinks.’ 
She warns you can also contract the infection ‘by having sex with someone who has it’ — which the NHS website says is especially common during unprotected anal and oral sex. 
 
   
Gastro symptoms can last for months on end (Picture: Getty Images) 
Daniel adds: ‘Giardiasis can be easily spread, particularly as some people can carry the infection without showing symptoms.  
‘When someone has contracted giardiasis, they are most infectious from the onset of symptoms, if any present, until around two days after they have stopped.’ 
Giardiasis treatment 
If you suspect you may have giardiasis, you should visit your GP, who will likely arrange a stool sample to confirm infection. 
After this, Daniel explains treatment ‘is usually in the form of antibiotics to treat the infection, alongside plenty of fluids to reduce the risk of dehydration.’

British company UKSOL, selling its one-panel kit for £699, has become the first supplier to meet regulatory compliance for the devices.



The 460W panels are on sale for delivery through Argos, and for pick-up and delivery with City Plumbing – a builders’ merchant with 350 branches.





More retailers are expected to make plug-in solar products available in the coming weeks, after new rules allowing their sale in the UK came into force on Thursday.



Wickes and Currys join plug-in solar rush



Wickes said it would be making plug-in solar available to its customers “in the coming weeks”.



Currys said it was working to make these products “available to UK households as soon as possible, including through both our website and larger stores”.

West Point’s only climate scientist fired after continuing to teach human causes of climate change


Adam Kalkstein compared administration’s order to ‘trying to teach the law’ without mentioning ‘the constitution’




The only climate scientist teaching at West Point, the US army’s military academy, was fired after he resisted an order to stop teaching about the human causes of the climate emergency, a lawsuit claims.
Dr Adam Kalkstein, a civilian professor of geography at the New York institution, was terminated after the spring semester this year, six months after a testy meeting with Brig Gen Shane Reeves, then dean of West Point’s academic board, the court filing said.

According to Kalkstein, who taught army cadets there for 17 years, he told the dean at a November 2025 meeting that an order to cut from the curriculum content about the human causes of climate change was immoral and potentially illegal.
It “would be like trying to teach the law without being able to even mention the constitution,” he said.


Reeves responded by “storming out” of the meeting after telling Kalkstein that Donald Trump was commander in chief, and set the agenda for West Point, the lawsuit alleged.
The developments were reported on Wednesday by Stars and Stripes, and the New York Times.
Kalkstein’s lawsuit is the second legal action over the stifling of academic freedoms filed by an educator at West Point.
Tim Bakken, the academy’s longest-serving law professor, had a similarly fiery meeting with a uniformed colonel, John Gregory, last year after standing up to a new Trump administration policy ordering civilian colleagues to seek approval before publishing papers or giving speeches, the Washington Post reported in July.
According to Bakken’s lawsuit, Gregory ordered him to “stop talking and sit down” during a meeting of dozens of faculty members. “We’re a military institution. We follow orders,” Gregory is alleged to have said.
The US Military Academy, West Point’s formal name, dropped its challenge to a preliminary injunction against the policy obtained by Bakken’s lawyers this month, military.com reported, and the parties have agreed “in principle” to work towards a permanent solution.


Kalkstein’s attorney, Michael Sussman, told the Times that his client is a conservative Republican who believes military students need to know the truth about the causes of the climate crisis as a matter of national security.
“He is loyal to the cadets and the academy,” he said. “And to his perspective, edicts that he can’t say what’s true in a classroom is beyond his tolerance and totally counterproductive.”

We’ve seen wildfires burn down homes and now face the risk of flash floods as we move into autumn. It should be a wake-up call for those saying that concerns about the climate crisis are overblown; that we should simply sit back and do nothing; or row back on attempts to restore our natural environment. As the new environment secretary, I won’t let that happen.

articles.title: Plug-in solar panels are coming to a shop near you - here's what to know
articles.raw_rss: The UK government claimes panels could help homes "significantly cut" energy bills.
articles.raw_meta: The UK government claimes panels could help homes "significantly cut" energy bills.
articles.jina_text:
Plug-in solar panels will be hitting the shelves of DIY shops and High Street retailers after the government changed the rules to allow them to be legally sold in the UK.
They are significantly cheaper than roof panels, can be installed without an electrician and are suitable for properties with outdoor space, including some balconies.
Retailers including Argos will be stocking products from Thursday, and the government expects other shops to follow suit. 
It hopes plug-in solar panels will help households save money and reduce reliance on overseas fuel sources, the price of which has fluctuated in recent months due to the Middle East conflict.
Customers should get their wiring checked by a professional to ensure it is safe before parting with cash, experts say.


Will plug-in solar panels save me money?
The government hopes the plug-in panels will offer people a more affordable way into solar energy compared to roof installation, although savings will be lower because they generate less power.














A one-panel kit will cost £699 while a two-panel kit will be £1,089, according to UK solar company UKSOL.
The current regulations only allow people to plug in one device per property, but this may be changed in future. A single device may include more than one panel.
The government expects prices to settle at £400-£600 as competition increases and more products are developed.
Its research shows a household could save between £70 and £110 a year on their energy bills.
The precise amount will depend on how the panels are orientated and how long they run. An unshaded south-facing spot is best.
Households which use energy during daylight hours will benefit most as the electricity must be used as it is generated. 
Any power not consumed will flow back to the grid, but it's unlikely homes will get any cash for this.
Unlike rooftop solar panels, these systems do not need to be certified under the official Microgeneration Certification Scheme (MCS), which is the UK's official quality mark for small-scale renewable energy systems.





But it also means they will not normally qualify for the Smart Export Guarantee that pays people for excess solar power.

UKSOL
One of the UKSOL plug-in solar panels
How much energy can they generate?
The panels will make a difference to a household's power consumption but it is deliberately modest for safety reasons.
While kits may come with panels that are capable of generating more power, the microinverter - which turns the current from the panel into electricity homes can use - will limit output to the home to 800 watts. 
That's enough to cover "always-on" electrical appliances such as fridges and devices left on standby. The government says it should power about a fifth of the average household's electricity use while the sun is shining.

articles.title: Michael Sheen hopes 'extraordinary' reaction to toxic waste documentary spurs action
articles.raw_rss: Dozens of people contacted BBC Wales following coverage of Sheen's investigation into chemical giant Monsanto.
articles.raw_meta: Dozens of people contacted BBC Wales following coverage of Sheen's investigation into chemical giant Monsanto.
articles.jina_text:
Michael Sheen has welcomed the reaction to his documentary investigating Wales' toxic waste legacy, saying he hopes it pushes the relevant authorities to "find a solution".
Dozens of people contacted BBC Wales following coverage of Sheen's investigation into chemical giant Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
One of them was a former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping to seal toxic waste underground and said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.
Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond to either Sheen and his team or the BBC when asked to comment.
Asked about the response to the documentary, Sheen said he wanted "to see something actually happen".
"So getting a response was a really important part of it, and hoping that response would push the people who are in positions to get on with it," he said.
Sheen said he had received "extraordinary messages" from people who wanted to tell their stories and how they had been affected.
"There's a lot of stuff for us to follow up," he said.
Sheen said he hoped "people in the more official areas" would respond as well and "work with us on it".
"We want to find a solution rather than something that keeps putting people in a position where they have to put breaks on because they can't afford to get involved in this, so we really want to find a solution to this."



Buried with Michael Sheen

17 August 2026
Watch on iPlayer

What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales.




Much of the documentary focuses on researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan, who tried to raise the alarm about 14 sites - 12 of which were in Wales - but died before his warnings were heeded.
"What he told me made my blood run cold," said Sheen, who spoke to Gowan months before he died.
Gowan, a former farming consultant, alleged that chemical giant Monsanto had dumped "huge amounts of industrial chemicals all around Wales".
Following coverage of the documentary, people contacted BBC Wales to speak about their experience, including Stephen Constance, 61, who worked at Monsanto's Newport factory in the 1990s.
He described working for the company as "absolutely dreadful".
Natural Resources Wales previously said "the legacy of historic industrial activity" in the UK and globally was an issue, most of which "took place before modern environmental regulations were in place", the "records can be limited and the nature of waste is not always fully known".
The Welsh government previously said that "addressing contaminated land" was a key priority.

Our buildings are monuments to extraction and extreme emissions. But what if we turned from destructive concrete to timber? 
 
 
Last chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% off. Click here to order 













 
 

I travelled to Oslo in the early autumn. It felt like arriving into the future. Or, at least, a fragment of a possible future. I drove north in the quiet digital bubble of my electric rental car. In 2024, Norway became the first country in the world where electric cars outnumbered petrol cars.
A smooth, pristine motorway unfolded between farmlands and low hillsides of dense green forest. Long tunnels carried the route up above the banks of Lake Mjøsa, Norway’s largest lake. After a little more than an hour, the road curved downward to run parallel to the lakeshore.
Through gaps in a line of golden birch trees, a tall, slim structure broke the horizon. It rose from the water’s edge, topped by a triangular crown of bare, interlocking beams. Against the heavy grey sky and the enfolding mist, it radiated a gentle warmth from its pale burnt-orange exterior. The only building of any height anywhere in the surrounding landscape, it is known as Mjøstårnet, the “Tower of Mjøsa”: an 18-storey, 277ft (84m)-high wooden skyscraper. The tallest all-timber building in the world.
Mjøstårnet occupies a slice of shoreline next to the small town of Brumunddal. It incorporates offices, apartments, and a 72-room hotel. I was staying on the 11th floor, and I rode up in an elevator shaft fabricated entirely of wood (although the elevator cabin itself was made of steel and glass).


View image in fullscreen
The interior of Mjøstårnet. Photograph: Voll Arkitekter
Two sides of my corner room had large picture windows, one looking west across the lake and the other north along the shore. There were wooden floors throughout, wooden tables and lamps, a wooden bed, and pair of low swivel chairs formed out of thin slats of bent pinewood.
Most striking of all was the huge wooden column that formed both the corner piece of the room and – extending in segments above and below me – one of the four edge-points of the whole tower. It looked reassuringly sturdy, as if it were the trunk of a massive tree that had been stripped of its bark and worked into a smoothed organic approximation of a geometric strut of steel or concrete. Which is almost exactly the case: except that it is not just one tree but many – a series of blocks of timber that are precision cut and then pressed and held together using extremely strong glue, creating what is known as mass timber, or glulam (short for “glued laminated timber”).
The piece in my room was the largest of its kind in the building, its cross-section measuring some 2ft wide by 5ft (0.6m by 1.5m) long. Although coated in a pale wax laminate, you could still see the unique knots and whorls running across its composite slices of wood.

Japan killed 14,000 bears after a rise in deadly attacks on people – but will it work?


Bears killed 13 people in Japan last year, as a lack of forest foods increased conflicts. Yet some say the country’s controversial cull could threaten the endangered species




Every summer, millions of people escape the heat and humidity of Tokyo by heading to the tranquil resort town of Karuizawa in Japan’s Nagano prefecture – just an hour by bullet train from the capital. Here, at the foot of Mount Asama, visitors stroll bamboo-lined pathways, cycle in verdant highlands, and practise the wellness ritual of shinrin-yoku, bathing among the cool hinoki forests. It would be the ideal nature retreat – if it wasn’t for the bears.
From June to August, bears often move close to Karuizawa, feeding on the mulberries, ants, leaves and cherry blossoms that grow near the town. Unlike nuts, these foods are low in calories, spurring the bears to seek out further sustenance. “They’re more likely to get close to residential spaces to see what they can find,” says Amelia Hiorns, a British zoologist who previously worked with Picchio Wildlife Research Centre in the town. “This combines with the busiest season for tourists.”

Picchio, a small Japanese conservation and nature education group, has been working to improve coexistence between bears and people in Karuizawa and the surrounding region since the 1990s. Staff respond to reported bear sightings with one of their three Karelians – a dog breed trained in the western US to chase away bears. When dogs aren’t enough, the Picchio team tranquilises and relocates bears deep in the forest.


View image in fullscreen
Junta Imura, a member of Picchio’s bear team, in forests near Karuizawa in Nagano prefecture. His Karelian dog, Elf, is trained to chase bears away. Photograph: Picchio Wildlife Research Center
Today, Karuizawa’s approach has few parallels in Japan, as conflicts between bears and humans surge to unprecedented levels across the country.
Last year, bears attacked more than 230 people in the country, with 13 people killed, making it the deadliest year on record. Most attacks were in the mountainous northern prefectures of Akita and Iwate, where record-breaking heat affected the growth of beech nuts and acorns that bears rely on to fatten up for hibernation. Diminished human populations in Japan’s rural hinterlands, with orchards and woodlands left abandoned, exacerbated the situation as bears descended into villages in search of food.

articles.jina_text:
British farmers have faced a sweltering summer tested by heatwaves, wildfires and water shortages – but a bumper berry harvest could prove a rare bright spot.
With two-thirds of the harvest now picked, this year’s haul is 6% up on last year’s already unusually large crop, according to British Berry Growers (BBG). Volumes of blackberries, blueberries and raspberries picked have been particularly strong, the trade body said.

The hot conditions have helped the berries grow rapidly and most UK berry crops are grown under polytunnels in the UK on drip irrigation, insulating them from the punishing heat, the trade body said.
There are, however, fears late season strawberry production will be slower than hoped in early autumn as plants become exhausted from heavy cropping during the heatwave, while blackcurrant production is expected to be down 10%.
Much of Britain has sweltered under a record five heatwaves this year and endured drought and wildfires, with the hot, dry conditions damaging crops and reducing yields of domestic produce.


View image in fullscreen
Farmers in the UK have faced challenging conditions this summer.  Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty Images
Nick Marston, the chair of the BBG, said: “British growers have collectively invested millions of pounds over many years to improve resilience to these conditions.


“That includes developing secure water supplies, from winter storage reservoirs to highly efficient, computer-controlled drip irrigation systems that deliver water precisely where it’s needed.
“The hot weather could reduce the size of fruit as berries ripen sooner but the industry had a good start to the season with a dull April and May and berries remained within supermarket specifications.”
In 2024, it was predicted that two-fifths of British growers of strawberries and raspberries could go out of business by the end of 2026. However, growers have since experienced consecutive strong summers.
But the summer has been difficult for other UK food producers exposed to climate crisis-driven heatwaves.
The UK’s cereals harvest has also been hit by the weather, with wheat 13% below the five-year average, according to the latest report from the government-backed Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB). Spring barley yields are expected to be about a quarter below the five-year average and the lowest since comparable records began in 1999.
Anthony Hopkins, AHDB’s director of cereals and oilseeds, said: “The cumulative effect of successive poor harvests will be placing immense financial pressure on many arable businesses right now.”

ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records




More than 40,000 extra people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than would be expected in normal temperatures, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday.
The figures do not include this summer, when England has sweltered under a succession of heatwaves and is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.

The number of people dying prematurely due to high temperatures is expected to rise further as the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels continues to push up temperatures and the population ages. Elderly people, as well as children and the unwell, are particularly vulnerable to heat.
Emergency departments in England’s hospitals have experienced their busiest period ever this summer, with almost 2.5 million patients attending A&E each month in May, June and July and the heat cited as a main reason. Nurses were collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, their union warned earlier in August.

This summer’s heatwaves and wildfires were “immediate, real-world manifestations of the climate emergency”, the groups said, making reform of transport – responsible for more carbon emissions than any other sector in the UK – an urgent priority.

There are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hope 
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 













 
 
The news is very often about the bad things (especially if you’re on the Guardian’s environment desk). Wildfires, floods, tipping points, billionaires making huge profits and buying themselves island refuges for the apocalypse … And yet, ticking along beside that is the steady pulse of what the rest of humanity is doing in response to the climate crisis. From housing developments with no cars to buildings made out of hemp, all over the planet people are ploughing ahead and changing their neighbourhoods and cities and the world.

But as news stories typically need to be about new developments or things people didn’t previously know about, it can be hard to cover all those brilliant initiatives being undertaken in the background – no matter how cheering they are. Which is why, back in 2023, we decided to ignore the usual rules about what constitutes “news” and start writing about them anyway. Readers, we knew, would like to hear about them.


And so was born the Alternatives, a weekly news column where we cover these different projects. We’re constantly amazed by some of the things we learn. Norway has heat pumps in two-thirds of its homes. China’s sponge cities are targeting 70% rainwater reuse. Paris is building a gigantic cooling machine using river water. It feels as if the series is a vast chronicle of the transformations that are taking place everywhere, far faster than we sometimes realise.
This year, as part of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign, we are highlighting all of the work that our environment team does to bring readers positive ideas such as those above, providing hope that a better world is possible if we start acting on it.
So, we asked our environment reporters around the world to share one big idea from their journalism – funded by you – that has helped drive or inspire some kind of positive change for the planet. Their answers are below.
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 


Petra Stock
Climate and environment reporter, Guardian Australia
Many objections to wind turbines cite the impact on wildlife, such as birds and bats. But there are simple fixes and innovations that demonstrate there doesn’t need to be a trade-off between clean energy and safeguarding biodiversity. One such approach I reported – which involves raising the “cut in” speed at which turbines start spinning – has the potential to save tens of thousands of native bats every year, with minimal impact on energy output.
